statements.quote: We refer to these initial sentences as the “initial prompt,” which we observe.

We observe both the initial AI-generated text and the final job post text posted to the market. In addition to freely editing the post, the employer was shown options for how the AI could edit the job post for them. These “personalization” options were “Make it casual,” “Make it formal,” “Shorten it,” “Add more details,” “Rewrite it.” We observe use of these personalization editing options. We also observe the time the employer spent on the job post writing process.
statements.locator: PDF p. 10, Section 3.1, final paragraph before Section 3.2.

statements.quote: The primary dataset used in our analysis includes all job posts made by employers in the experimental sample from the time they were assigned to the experiment up until August 3, 2023, which is 14 days post-allocation. We compile job post-level data encompassing all posts, applications, and hires occurring within 14 days of the posting date. We track the complete evolution of job posts from conception to submission. For each treated job post, we observe: (1) the employer’s initial prompt to the AI system, (2) the AI-generated first draft, (3) all subsequent employer modifications, and (4) the final published version. This granular tracking allows us to analyze not just outcomes, but the entire production of the job post.

statements.quote: The dataset we use in this analysis consists of all job posts posted by employers in the experimental sample between the moment they were allocated into the experiment and June 6, 2023 when allocation stopped. We construct job post-level data with all posts, applications, and hires they have within 14 days of posting. While in general we are interested in many outcomes related to posting and hiring, for these purposes we primarily want to 1) show that the take-up in this experiment was comparable with the main experiment and then 2) use the employer histories to understand if there is non-random selection into take-up.

notes:
The whole 161,417-character markdown conversion (1,463 lines), including Appendices A and B, was read in contiguous chunks. The source is the 72-page authors' draft dated September 4, 2026, titled 'More, but Worse: The Marketplace Effects of AI-Generated Job Posts', previously 'Generative AI and Labor Market Matching Efficiency'. PDF text was checked for the quoted statements, and all PDF external hyperlinks were extracted.

No statement offering public data or code, data-on-request promise, preregistration link, or separate supplementary-file deposit was found. The statements above document the authors' observed data and the paper's illustrative materials; they do not establish that these data are publicly accessible. Both data_url and code_url in forms/c635.json are empty.

All external links in the paper were checked with Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1. PDF p. 1: https://emmawiles.github.io/storage/jobot.pdf returned HTTP 200 after redirecting to http://www.emmawiles.com/storage/jobot.pdf; its 1,546,906 bytes have the same SHA-256 digest as the saved PDF. PDF p. 45: https://nationalequityatlas.org/indicators/Wages_Median returned HTTP 200 and is the background median-wage indicator, not data from any randomized study in this paper.

Publisher/working-paper landing page https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5187344 returned HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenge. Stopped there; no login, account, access request, or bot-check bypass was attempted. Its supplementary-file availability could not be assessed.

Author fallback checks: https://john-joseph-horton.com/papers/generative-ai-and-labor-market-matching-efficiency/ returned HTTP 200 and lists only the paper PDF under Paper links; https://www.emmawiles.com/ and https://www.emmawiles.com/research/ returned HTTP 200. The research page explicitly identifies both titles as the same paper and links the PDF and media coverage without a data/code/supplement link. https://www.emmawiles.com/storage/jobot.pdf returned HTTP 200 (1,546,906 bytes; 72 pages; September 4, 2026). The first-author homepage identifies her former name as Emma van Inwegen, which was also searched.

The unrelated OSF registration https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/hsy2k/ returned HTTP 200. Its title and description establish that it concerns knowledge workers using ChatGPT on technical tasks, not the employers' job-post experiments. It and the unrelated Seattle minimum-wage and resume-writing records are excluded from deposits.

The PDF contains an illustrative employer prompt and generated draft on p. 10 and stylized interfaces in Figures 1 and 17 (pp. 11 and 70). Footnote 27 (p. 47) points to example posts in Appendix A.8, but that section (pp. 55-63) contains tables and figures, not the promised example-post collection. These in-paper illustrations and aggregate tables are not a participant-level data deposit.

No matching public deposit was identified, so no dataset columns or row counts could be inspected and no study-level public data coverage is confirmed for S1, S2, or S3 (S4 is a nonrandomized subset of S1). Nothing found would resolve final.open_items on the account-to-person mapping, the implemented similarity reference pool, similarity-sample exclusions and arm counts, or skill-count construction. No additional per-person means, SDs, SEs, analyzed counts, or diversity measures can be computed from public row-level data located in this check.

Confidence is medium: all four named repository search APIs were searched successfully using both titles and the first author's current/former names, with broader name searches and OSF contributor listings, but SSRN was blocked and unindexed deposits cannot be ruled out. 'none_found' records the search result; it does not assert that the authors' underlying data are unavailable under every possible arrangement.
